conversation.content:
Hello! I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a quick, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS). It helps us spot common mood-and-anxiety symptoms that can show up in the first weeks and months postpartum—nothing you say will leave this room without your permission, and there are no “right” answers.

We’ll walk through 10 short questions about the past seven days. If any item feels hard to talk about, we can pause or reword it—your comfort is the priority. Ready to start?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very often. I can usually tell when something is supposed to be funny—like when my husband sends me a silly meme—but I don’t feel that spark to actually laugh. Most of the time I just give a little smile or nod, and then my mind drifts back to the baby or the chores. If I had to pick, I’d say “not much.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed out loud this week. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat now. I’ll think, “That’s supposed to be funny,” but I still feel this heavy, tired feeling. So, “no, not much at all.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a new show, even just a quiet shower—but lately it feels like I’m just dragging myself toward everything. When I think about plans, my first feeling is “ugh, more effort,” not real excitement.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right or my milk isn’t good enough. When he had a little diaper rash last week, I kept replaying every change in my head, convinced it was my fault for not catching it sooner. Even tiny stuff, like spilling a bottle, makes me feel like I’m failing at being his mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—so I jump up to check his breathing. Then I start spiraling about whether the room’s too cold, or if I sterilized the bottles right, or what if he gets sick and I don’t notice in time. Nothing specific triggered it; it just feels like there’s always a low-level hum of “what if something bad happens?” running in the background.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that happens too. Sometimes out of nowhere I’ll get this rush—like my chest tightens and I feel I can’t catch my breath. It feels silly because nothing’s actually wrong: the baby’s fine, the apartment’s quiet, but for a minute I’m convinced something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and even more tired.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is already looming, plus the laundry pile keeps growing and I can’t remember the last time I ate a real meal. I’ll sit down for a second and suddenly think of five other things I “should” be doing. I’m getting through the essentials, but it’s like I’m constantly treading water and barely keeping my head up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain just keeps circling—did I burp him long enough, did I lock the door, am I already failing at this mom thing? Some nights I finally drift off, then I jolt awake sure I heard him cry (and sometimes he’s still asleep). It’s like the sadness and the worries tag-team me the second the lights go out.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel that way most of the day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at the baby and feel so much love, but right behind it is this heavy sadness I can’t shake. Little tasks feel huge, and sometimes I just sit there staring out the window feeling empty. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m okay—but the miserable feeling just sits in my chest anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. It’s usually when I’m alone—like last night when I couldn’t get him to latch and I just felt so useless I burst into tears. Or yesterday when I spilled the pumped milk on the counter; I sat on the kitchen floor and cried like it was the worst thing in the world. Afterwards I feel a little relief, but it keeps happening over small stuff that normally wouldn’t make me sob.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I haven’t wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, self-referred for mood concerns.

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS-relevant):  
<sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>free-floating anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic episodes</sym>, <sym>sleep-onset difficulty</sym>, <sym>frequent tearfulness</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>.  
No self-harm ideation.

Pattern: Persistent sadness, cognitive self-blame, and somatic anxiety present most days, interfering with functioning and rest.  
Risk factors: First-time mom, sleep deprivation, feeding difficulties, absence of psychosocial supports mentioned.

Screening observation: Responses exceed threshold for clinically significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; safety risk low at present. Recommend formal assessment (EPDS total score ≥ likely 15–17) and expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty for evaluation and care planning.
